title: Being typecast as a ragtime pianist
summary: Hug discusses the ragtime tag and the difficulty of playing it in cocktail lounges.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: That's kind of brings us into my next point very naturally. You're known internationally, basically, as a ragtime pianist. Do you think that this is an apt description of your style? I'm sure it limits your range to call you a ragtime pianist. What do you think of the tag personally, though?

Yes, I think the tag ragtime is sort of put me in a certain category that has been hard for me to overcome from lots of directions. The people who traditionally like ragtime don't like to hear me play anything else. And, of course, I don't play in a strict progressive sense. That's okay. But I would say that just saying that I'm a ragtime piano player, while I feel very flattered to have been included in this category with many of the real ragtime greats, I think I went a little beyond that because I didn't stop there. In other words, I feel this way, that if you're a pianist, you play piano. If you're a musician, you play music. For instance, I think Will Hines could probably play ragtime if he wanted to. I think Teddy Wilson could probably play ragtime. He may not be really a real traditionalist, but I think that they could play ragtime if they really wanted to. And I think that they've gone beyond that and they've gone through different phases.

Certainly, I don't see any harm in keeping up with some of the things that are going on. I think it's kind of ironic that you say the people who like to hear you play ragtime like little else, and it must cause a problem on a job, because most people don't come to the night to the average cocktail lounge to hear ragtime, which is a problem. That's right. Would you like to play more ragtime in the cocktail work where you're limited to playing very little of it? You often feel the urge to play more, even though it's incompatible with the kind of mild surroundings of a cocktail lounge.

Well, it's very funny, Charlie, that you ask me that, because lots of times I did feel as though I was being done an injustice. When I was at the height of my build-up as a Dixieland pianist and as a ragtime pianist, I was not able to really play this kind of music as I wanted to. And I was hoping, this was about, I guess, say maybe 10, 15 years ago, that I could have been working in places where I could have really just maybe stuck to this particular type of music and either became known as one type of pianist or another. But as you said, it is very difficult because, as you know, when you're working in a public place, you get all types of people, all tastes of music, and you sort of have to go along with the public. I don't have to tell you that. You know, you're playing right now with a little group, and you all go along sort of with the public. I mean, if they want a particular thing, well, you play it for them. And this is what I try to do. Now, I don't know if I would be very happy just playing ragtime. Maybe I would. I don't know. If I would probably maybe be getting paid enough for it, if I was in the right kind of a place and so forth, maybe I would be satisfied just to play ragtime. Or, as a lot of people say, Dixieland, I feel quite flattered when people come in and say, well, we've heard so much about you as a Dixieland jazz piano player, you know? Well, this is very flattering because, as I said before, there's no greater compliment to be paid you to say you are highly rated as a Dixieland musician.
